title: Production scenarios (cross-cutting)
scopeHtml: Combined JVM + GC + concurrency + diagnosis incidents, spot-the-bug, migrations and post-incident reviews. Mostly scenarios; four concept questions anchor the method.

questions.promptHtml: A Java pod has a 2 GiB memory limit and -Xmx1536m. Heap usage never exceeds 1 GiB, yet Kubernetes keeps OOMKilling it. How can that happen, and what does the container limit actually count?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you know the heap is only one slice of process memory, and that the kernel (not the JVM) decides the kill.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The cgroup limit applies to the whole process RSS, not the heap. Metaspace, thread stacks, code cache, direct buffers, GC structures and malloc arenas all sit outside -Xmx. If the heap can grow to 1.5 GiB and the rest needs 600 MB, we cross 2 GiB and the kernel OOM killer sends SIGKILL, so there is no Java exception and no heap dump. I size the heap to about 50-75% of the limit and verify the rest with NMT."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
container limit 2048 MiB  (cgroup memory.max)
 |- Java heap (up to -Xmx)            1536   <- the only part -Xmx caps
 |- Metaspace (class metadata)        ~100-300
 |- Thread stacks (N x -Xss, 1 MiB default on 64-bit Linux)   200 threads = ~200
 |- Code cache (JIT output)           up to 240 (ReservedCodeCacheSize default with tiered)
 |- GC data (remembered sets, card tables, mark bitmaps)   several % of heap, G1 more
 |- Direct ByteBuffers / Netty pools  bounded by MaxDirectMemorySize (defaults to ~ Xmx)
 |- Native libs, malloc arenas, mmap'd files, JVM internals
  • Since JDK 10 the JVM reads cgroup limits (container support is on by default); -XX:MaxRAMPercentage (default 25) sets max heap as a % of the container limit. Only the heap is bounded by it.
  • OOMKilled shows Exit code 137, Reason: OOMKilled; the JVM never gets to run HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError.
  • The kill is triggered by RSS (plus page cache charged to the cgroup) crossing the limit, so "heap looks fine" proves nothing.
  • Diagnose with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary then jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary, plus Micrometer jvm.buffer.memory.used, jvm.memory.used{area=nonheap}, and container RSS from cAdvisor.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# sane starting point for a 2 GiB pod (measure, then tune)
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60
-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=256m
-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary
-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Setting -Xmx equal to the container limit.
  • Watching only heap dashboards; alerting on container RSS vs limit is what predicts the kill.
  • Assuming a bigger limit fixes it when the cause is a native leak: it only delays the kill.
  • Setting -Xms == -Xmx and forgetting that G1 then commits all of it immediately.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why no stack trace? → SIGKILL from the kernel; the JVM cannot catch it. Evidence is in kubectl describe pod and dmesg.
  2. Does MaxRAMPercentage include metaspace? → No, heap only.
  3. How would you find a leak that NMT shows as "Internal" or "Other"? → Take two NMT baselines (VM.native_memory baseline / summary.diff); if it is outside the JVM (JNI, glibc arenas), use MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2, jemalloc/tcmalloc profiling, or async-profiler nativemem (verify version support).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "native memory is also used." Senior: itemizes each region, gives the sizing formula (limit = heap + metaspace + stacks + code cache + direct + ~10-20% slack), and sets up NMT diffs and RSS alerting before the incident.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service moved from VMs to 2 GiB pods with -Xmx copied from the VM config and died every few hours under load; the missing ingredient was 400 threads x 1 MiB stacks plus Netty direct buffers.

questions.contextHtml: A payment-quote service (Java 17, 4 pods, 4 vCPU each, ~1,200 RPS total) is rolled out with a normal rolling update. Steady-state p99 is 90 ms. For about 3 minutes after each new pod becomes Ready, that pod shows p99 of 1.8-2.5 s and CPU at 380%; then it settles. Error rate is 0 but the upstream gateway times out at 1 s, so 4-6% of requests fail during every deploy. GC logs show young pauses of 15-20 ms, nothing unusual. The readiness probe is a TCP check on the port.
questions.promptHtml: Why only after deploy, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more pods / bigger CPU / tune GC." That ignores that the problem is time-boxed to a fresh JVM and that GC is healthy.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the same happen on a pod restart with no code change (confirms warmup, not the new build)? Is traffic shifted to the pod immediately at Ready (load balancer ramp)? Any CPU limit lower than the request (throttling)? Are there lazy caches/connection pools filled on first use?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Slow the rollout (maxSurge=1, maxUnavailable=0, minReadySeconds=120) and make the gateway retry on another pod with a budget. This hides the symptom while I fix it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) JIT warmup: code starts in the interpreter, then C1, then C2; compiler threads burn the CPU (380%) while request threads run slow code. (b) Class loading/initialization and lazy framework wiring on first requests. (c) Cold caches/connection pools (first DB/HTTP handshakes). (d) CPU throttling of compiler threads by the cgroup quota. Red herring: GC, which is fine.
  4. How I'd verify each: jcmd <pid> Compiler.queue and -XX:+PrintCompilation (or JFR jdk.Compilation events) during the window; jstat -compiler/-printcompilation; CPU by thread (top -H) showing C2 CompilerThre hot; -Xlog:class+load counts; container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total in Prometheus; JFR comparison of a cold vs 10-minute-old pod.
  5. Root cause: The pod receives its full share of traffic while hot methods are still interpreted (roughly 10-50x slower than C2 output) and the compiler threads compete with request threads for 4 vCPUs. A TCP readiness probe says "port open", not "ready to serve at speed".
  6. Fix: Short term: warmup endpoint/startup task that replays ~5-10k synthetic requests through the hot paths before readiness flips true; load-balancer slow-start (e.g. ramp from 10% to 100% over 3 min). Long term: AppCDS to cut class-load time (does not warm the JIT), CRaC (a checkpoint/restore with pre-warmed state, requires a supporting JDK distribution; verify support) or GraalVM native image if the deployment model allows. Give the pod a CPU request equal to its limit during startup (or use startup burst CPU where the platform supports it).
// warmup before readiness: exercise real code paths, not a no-op
@EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent.class)
void warm() {
  for (int i = 0; i < 8_000; i++) quoteService.quote(sampleRequest(i % 50));
  readiness.markReady();
}
  1. Prevention: A deploy-time SLO check on the first 5 minutes of each pod, a canary step with traffic ramp, and a test in CI that measures p99 of the first N seconds after boot.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not -Xcomp or aggressive lowered compile thresholds in prod (huge compile storm, worse). Not disabling tiered compilation. Warmup traffic must not hit real side effects (payments) and must be idempotent/synthetic.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Pods autoscale up during a spike, so warmup hits at the worst time. → Keep headroom (scale earlier on CPU 50%), use slow-start, or pre-warm via CRaC snapshot.
  • Warmup passes but p99 is still bad on the first minute. → Check C2 deopt storms (-Xlog:deoptimization*=debug, verify flag per JDK) due to type-profile pollution from warmup data unlike prod.
  • Is native image the answer? → It removes warmup but peak throughput is usually lower (no profile-guided C2 unless PGO is used), and reflection/proxy config costs; evaluate per service.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team "fixed" deploy spikes by adding replicas; the spike stayed because each new pod was equally cold. A 90-second warmup gate and a 2-minute LB slow-start cut deploy errors from 5% to near zero.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames GC or asks for more hardware.
  • Hire: identifies JIT/cold start, adds readiness warmup and traffic ramp.
  • Strong hire: separates JIT, class loading, caches and CPU throttling with evidence for each, and discusses AppCDS vs CRaC vs native image trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml: A Netty-based gateway (Java 17, G1) runs in a 3 GiB pod with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 (heap about 2.1 GiB). Every 6-9 hours a pod restarts with OOMKilled, exit code 137. Heap in Grafana peaks at 1.1 GiB, GC pauses under 30 ms, no OutOfMemoryError in the logs. Pod RSS climbs steadily from 1.9 GiB to 3.0 GiB over a few hours. The service proxies request bodies of 1-50 MB. It was upgraded last week from a library that used heap buffers to one using pooled direct buffers.
questions.promptHtml: Find the cause and fix it without a guess-and-restart loop.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the memory limit" or "heap is fine so it's a Kubernetes bug."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize set? Did RSS growth start with the library change? Does it correlate with large bodies? Is jvm.buffer.memory.used graphed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise the limit to 4 GiB or lower MaxRAMPercentage to 50 to buy time and add -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=512m so it fails loudly (OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memory) instead of silently being killed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Direct buffer leak or oversize pool (refcount not released); (b) unbounded pooled arenas caching large chunks; (c) glibc malloc arena fragmentation; (d) metaspace/thread growth. Heap, which looks fine, is a red herring.
  4. How I'd verify each: Enable NMT (-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary), jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline then summary.diff an hour later; Micrometer jvm.buffer.memory.used{id=direct} and jvm.buffer.count; Netty PooledByteBufAllocator.DEFAULT.metric(); leak detector -Dio.netty.leakDetection.level=advanced in staging; pmap -x to see growing anonymous mappings.
  5. Root cause: Large 50 MB bodies made the pooled allocator keep big chunks per arena, and a handler path (error branch) never called release(), so refcounts stayed above 0. Direct buffers live outside -Xmx, and since no limit was configured, MaxDirectMemorySize defaults roughly to the max heap, so 2.1 GiB of heap plus 2+ GiB of direct overshoots a 3 GiB pod. The GC never freed them, since the heap was not under pressure (cleaner runs only when the owning Java objects die).
  6. Fix: Short term: set explicit direct memory cap and sane arenas; Long term: release in finally/use ReferenceCountUtil.release, stream large bodies instead of aggregating, lower maxOrder/disable thread-local caches for big chunks.
ByteBuf buf = ctx.alloc().directBuffer(len);
try {
  process(buf);
} finally {
  ReferenceCountUtil.release(buf); // missing on the error path = the leak
}
  1. Prevention: Alert on RSS/limit > 85% and on jvm.buffer.memory.used slope; leak detector at paranoid in load tests; a budget table in the repo (heap + direct + stacks + metaspace <= 75% limit).
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not -XX:+DisableExplicitGC blindly (it breaks the cleaner path used by NIO to free direct memory on pressure). Not calling System.gc() on a timer. Capping direct memory turns a silent kill into a catchable error, which is the better failure mode.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• NMT shows "Other" growing, not "Internal". → That bucket includes direct ByteBuffer.allocateDirect; JDK 17 NMT tracks it under "Other". Compare with BufferPoolMXBean.
  • Would heap dump help? → Rarely for native; it shows DirectByteBuffer objects and their cleaner, which can identify who holds them via MAT dominator tree.
  • Could it be page cache? → Yes in cgroups v1/v2 file-backed pages count toward the limit but are reclaimable; check memory.stat (anon vs file).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A proxy was killed every 7 hours; the fix was one missing release() on a 413-reject path that only large uploads hit.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases limits only.
  • Hire: names direct buffers and NMT, sets a cap.
  • Strong hire: finds the unreleased-buffer path, explains why GC did not help, adds the budget and alerting.

questions.contextHtml: An order service (Java 17, Spring MVC, Tomcat 200 threads) has a shared Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16) named appPool used for parallel enrichment. At 9:05 traffic rises from 400 to 900 RPS. Latency climbs to 30 s, then every request times out. CPU is 4%. jstack shows 200 Tomcat threads in WAITING at CompletableFuture.get, and all 16 appPool threads also WAITING in Future.get, none doing work. Queue size of appPool (a LinkedBlockingQueue): 3,400. DB and downstream metrics are healthy.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what is happening and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase pool size to 100." That moves the cliff and may reproduce it later.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does a task running on appPool submit more tasks to appPool and wait? Are timeouts set on get()? Is there any other work (batch jobs) sharing that pool?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart/rolling restart is a temporary relief; shed load at the gateway; if possible temporarily raise appPool core size via a feature flag.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Thread-pool deadlock (parent tasks hold all 16 threads waiting for child tasks that sit in the queue); (b) a slow dependency holding threads (ruled out by healthy metrics, CPU 4%); (c) a lock or classic deadlock (jstack reports none); (d) queue unbounded masking overload.
  4. How I'd verify each: jcmd <pid> Thread.print x3 five seconds apart and compare; look for stacks appPool-N blocked in CompletableFuture.get or FutureTask.get called from task code; ThreadPoolExecutor metrics (active, queue.size, completed) via Micrometer ExecutorServiceMetrics: active=16 and completed flat = starvation deadlock.
  5. Root cause: Parent tasks occupy all workers and block for children queued behind them. Little progress is possible; at 400 RPS the pool happened to have spare workers, at 900 RPS all 16 became parents. The unbounded queue hides it until latency is 30 s.
// buggy: parent and child on the same bounded pool
CompletableFuture<Order> parent = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
  var a = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchA(id), appPool); // queued behind parents
  var b = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchB(id), appPool);
  return merge(a.join(), b.join());                               // blocks a worker
}, appPool);
  1. Fix: Short term: separate pools (parent vs leaf) or run leaf calls inline. Better: do not block in tasks, compose with thenCombine, put timeouts on everything (orTimeout(2, SECONDS)), and use a bounded queue with CallerRunsPolicy or abort-with-503.
return fetchAAsync(id).thenCombine(fetchBAsync(id), this::merge)
                      .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
  1. Prevention: A bulkhead per downstream, executor metrics/alerts for active == max && queue growing, a lint/review rule "no blocking get/join on the same executor you are running on", and a load test above peak.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not just a bigger pool (a deeper nesting or higher load recreates it). Not a cached unbounded pool (thread explosion). Virtual threads would reduce the pain but not remove the need for timeouts and bounds.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why CPU is 4% and not 100%? → Nothing runnable; every thread is parked.
  • ForkJoinPool handles this? → join() inside FJP can compensate/help-steal (ManagedBlocker for CompletableFuture.get), but fixed ThreadPoolExecutor cannot.
  • How to detect it in a test? → Pool of size 1, submit a nested blocking task with a 1-s timeout.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "temporary" shared pool added during a perf sprint was deadlocked within a week of a campaign launch; a 10-line metrics alert on active==max would have caught it in 2 minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases pool size.
  • Hire: recognizes pool-dependency deadlock, separates pools.
  • Strong hire: removes blocking, adds bounded queue, timeouts, metrics and a repro test.

questions.contextHtml: A Spring Boot service (Java 17, HikariCP maximumPoolSize=20, 8 pods, Postgres max_connections=300) starts logging HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms (total=20, active=20, idle=0, waiting=146). It began 10 minutes after a deploy that added a call to a partner API inside a @Transactional method. Partner p99 went from 200 ms to 6 s during the incident. DB CPU is 12%, query times are normal. Tomcat threads: 200 each, 190 busy.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening, what do you do right now, and how do you prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Raise pool size to 100" (8 x 100 = 800 > 300 DB limit, and the DB is idle anyway).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does each connection do while held? Is the HTTP call inside the transaction? Is Open-Session-in-View enabled? Is leakDetectionThreshold set?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the deploy or feature-flag the partner call; set a short client timeout (1 s) with circuit breaker; do not raise the pool.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Connections held while waiting on a slow non-DB call (transaction spans remote I/O); (b) leaked connections (not closed); (c) slow queries (ruled out: DB CPU 12%); (d) DB-side locks (check pg_stat_activity for idle-in-transaction).
  4. How I'd verify each: pg_stat_activity showing idle in transaction with large state_change age; thread dump showing threads inside RestTemplate.exchange under a TransactionInterceptor frame; Hikari metrics hikaricp_connections_active/pending/usage (usage histogram = hold time) and leakDetectionThreshold=10000 warnings with stack of the borrower.
  5. Root cause: Little's law: connections in use = arrival rate x hold time. With 6 s holds and 8 pods x 20 = 160 connections the sustainable rate is 160/6 = ~27 tx/s, far under the arrival rate. The pool queues, Tomcat threads block waiting for connections, and the whole service stalls though the DB is idle.
@Transactional                       // connection checked out here...
public void settle(long id) {
  Order o = repo.lock(id);
  partnerClient.confirm(o);          // ...held across a 6 s remote call
  o.markConfirmed();
}
  1. Fix: Short term: set timeouts (connect 500 ms, read 1.5 s), circuit-breaker the partner, shorten connectionTimeout to ~2 s to fail fast. Long term: call the partner outside the transaction (read, call, then a short write transaction), or use an outbox plus async worker.
  2. Prevention: Hikari leakDetectionThreshold, an alert on pending > 0 for 1 min, an architecture test forbidding HTTP clients inside @Transactional, spring.jpa.open-in-view=false.
  3. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Bigger pool shifts the load to the DB (context switching, memory per connection; typical sizing guidance is cores x 2 + spindles on the DB, as discussed in HikariCP's pool-sizing notes). Not catching and ignoring the timeout exception.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What changes if we use PgBouncer? → Transaction pooling decouples client pools from server connections, but long transactions still pin a server connection.
  • Why does a 30 s connectionTimeout hurt? → Requests wait 30 s holding Tomcat threads, amplifying the outage; fail fast.
  • A leaked connection vs slow hold: how to tell? → Leak: active stays pinned even at zero traffic; hold: usage drops when load drops.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An engineer raised a pool 20 to 200 in an incident, and the database then fell over from 1,600 connections; the actual bug was a remote call inside a transaction.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raises pool size.
  • Hire: finds the remote call in a transaction, applies timeouts.
  • Strong hire: does the Little's law math, restructures the transaction, adds leak detection and guardrails.

questions.contextHtml:
A metrics aggregator, deployed in production on Java 11 behind a 32-thread request pool, counts events per customer:

class Stats {
  private final Map<String, Long> counts = new HashMap<>();

  void record(String customer) {
    counts.merge(customer, 1L, Long::sum);
  }
  long total() { return counts.values().stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum(); }
}

Symptoms: totals are 3-8% below the number of requests under load; once a week one pod pegs a core at 100% with a thread stuck in HashMap.putVal/TreeNode frames and never recovers; a rare ConcurrentModificationException in total().
questions.promptHtml: What are the bugs, why are the symptoms so different, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "HashMap isn't thread safe, use Hashtable" with no mechanism, and no mention of the compound-action issue with ConcurrentHashMap either.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Exact JDK? (Java 7 resize could create a cyclic bucket list; Java 8 changed the transfer order but races remain.) Is counting approximate or exact? How is total() consumed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Swap the map for a ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> hot-patch; restart the spinning pod.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Lost updates: two threads read the same value in merge then both write; (b) a resize racing with inserts, corrupting the bin structure (infinite loop in a tree/linked bin traversal; a cyclic list was the classic Java 7 case); (c) iteration while mutating gives the CME; (d) visibility: no happens-before between threads, so total() may see stale values.
  4. How I'd verify each: jstack x3 on the spinning pod showing the same thread in HashMap frames while RUNNABLE; a JCStress or simple 32-thread test with 10M increments showing missing counts; heap dump to inspect the table for a loop; -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions not needed.
  5. Root cause: HashMap has no synchronization, atomicity or visibility guarantee. merge is read-modify-write across several non-atomic steps; resize relinks nodes without protection; the JMM allows each thread to see a different state. The 100% CPU spin is the observable symptom of a corrupted structure (undefined behavior, not a promised failure mode).
  6. Fix:
private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
void record(String c) { counts.computeIfAbsent(c, k -> new LongAdder()).increment(); }
long total() { return counts.values().stream().mapToLong(LongAdder::sum).sum(); }

ConcurrentHashMap.merge(c, 1L, Long::sum) is also atomic per key. total() is weakly consistent (not a snapshot), which is fine for metrics; for an exact snapshot you need a lock or a different design. 7. Prevention: Code review rule "shared mutable collection needs a named concurrency policy", @GuardedBy/ErrorProne GuardedBy checks, a stress test in CI. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Collections.synchronizedMap fixes atomic individual calls but not iteration, and serializes everything. Not Hashtable. Don't put blocking work inside compute* lambdas (it holds a bin lock).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Is ConcurrentHashMap.size() exact? → An estimate under concurrent updates; use mappingCount() for large maps.
  • AtomicLong vs LongAdder here? → LongAdder reduces contention on hot keys with a small read cost; AtomicLong if you need compare-and-set.
  • Does Java 8+ fix the infinite loop? → The classic cyclic list was changed by the order-preserving resize, but data corruption and lost updates remain possible, so never rely on it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "statistics" HashMap shared since a hackathon caused a 100% CPU pod once a week; it was blamed on GC for months until a thread dump showed the HashMap frames.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "use synchronized everywhere" without understanding.
  • Hire: ConcurrentHashMap plus atomic update.
  • Strong hire: separates lost update, corruption and visibility, and knows weak consistency of iteration.

questions.contextHtml: A team migrates a Spring Boot 3.2 service (Java 21, Tomcat) to virtual threads (spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true) to remove a 400-thread pool. Load test looked good. In production at 1,500 RPS, after 20 minutes throughput collapses to ~40 RPS, p99 goes to 20 s, CPU is 8%, and Tomcat accepts requests but they hang. Carrier threads: 4 (4 vCPUs). A vendor SDK, called on every request, does synchronized (this) { return httpClient.send(...); } taking 300-800 ms. DB pool: 30 connections, fine. A JFR recording shows many jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events with durations over 20 ms.
questions.promptHtml: Why did it collapse, and how do you recover and migrate safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Virtual threads are cheap, so add more of them" (the scheduler's carriers are the limit), or "roll back and never use them".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which JDK exactly (21 vs 24+)? Which libraries synchronize around blocking I/O? What is jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism and maxPoolSize? Did the load test use the real SDK?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the flag (platform threads) or raise -Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism/maxPoolSize as a stopgap. Note: in JDK 21, blocking while holding a monitor pins the virtual thread to its carrier; it does not compensate with another carrier.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Pinning: 4 carriers all pinned inside the synchronized block waiting on I/O, everything else queues; (b) a bounded resource (DB pool) used with unbounded virtual threads; (c) an infinite number of threads piling CPU-bound work (CPU is only 8%, so unlikely); (d) a thread-dump tooling gap, since jstack does not show virtual threads.
  4. How I'd verify each: jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json file.json (shows virtual threads); -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full (JDK 21) printing stacks when pinned threads block; JFR jdk.VirtualThreadPinned and jdk.VirtualThreadSubmitFailed; jcmd <pid> Thread.print to see the 4 ForkJoinPool-1-worker carriers parked in the SDK frames.
  5. Root cause: With JDK 21, a virtual thread that blocks inside synchronized stays mounted on its carrier. Four concurrent calls each holding a monitor for ~500 ms hold all four carriers; since they also contend on the same monitor (this), they serialize at ~2 calls/s per monitor holder. All other virtual threads wait for a carrier. The load test used a mock without synchronized.
  6. Fix: Short term: wrap the SDK call in a bounded executor of platform threads, or replace synchronized in forked code with ReentrantLock (works for owned code; not for the vendor's). Long term: upgrade to JDK 24+ where JEP 491 makes synchronized not pin (native frames and a few cases still pin), or ask the vendor to fix, and bound concurrency to the SDK with a Semaphore.
private final Semaphore sdkSlots = new Semaphore(32);
Response call(Req r) throws InterruptedException {
  sdkSlots.acquire();               // a virtual thread blocked here unmounts cleanly
  try { return vendor.send(r); } finally { sdkSlots.release(); }
}
  1. Prevention: Load test with real client libraries; JFR pinned-event alert in staging; a dependency audit for synchronized around I/O; jdk.tracePinnedThreads in pre-prod.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not blanket raising maxPoolSize to hundreds (it only temporarily masks the problem and brings back platform-thread cost). Not pooling virtual threads. Not migrating everything at once; migrate per endpoint.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Upgrade to 25 LTS and the problem disappears? → Mostly for synchronized (JEP 491 shipped in 24); still pinned: native/JNI frames and some class-init cases; verify the SDK.
  • Does ThreadLocal matter here? → Works with virtual threads but each one has its own copy; costly if you stash big objects per request.
  • How to see queued virtual threads? → There is no metric by default; JFR and the scheduler's JMX are limited, so watch throughput vs carriers.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A rollout passed all tests and failed at 20 minutes under production concurrency; the difference was a real vendor client with one synchronized, found in 10 minutes with the JSON thread dump.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cannot diagnose beyond "virtual threads are broken".
  • Hire: identifies pinning from the dump and gets around it.
  • Strong hire: gives JDK-version-specific reasoning (21 vs 24), uses a Semaphore, and designs a staged migration.

questions.contextHtml: A legacy WAR (Java 11, Tomcat 9, 6 GiB heap, -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m) is hot-redeployed twice a day by the release script instead of restarting Tomcat. After 4-5 redeploys the node fails with java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace. catalina.out contains The web application [shop] created a ThreadLocal with key of type [com.shop.RequestCtx$1] and a value of type [com.shop.RequestCtx] ... but failed to remove it when the web application was stopped. ... likely to create a memory leak. Metaspace after each redeploy rises by ~90 MB and never drops. Heap looks normal.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the mechanism and the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase MaxMetaspaceSize" or "Metaspace OOM means too many classes, restart more often".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the ThreadLocal static in app code or a shared lib in tomcat/lib? Do the pool threads outlive the app (they are the container's threads)? Any JDBC drivers or logging frameworks in the WAR? Is redeploy-in-place required or just habit?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart Tomcat on each release (drains and clears everything); alert on loaded class count growth.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) ThreadLocal value (an instance of an app class) kept in a container worker thread's ThreadLocalMap; (b) JDBC driver registered in DriverManager by the parent loader; (c) an app thread or Timer not stopped; (d) static references from a shared-classpath library. Heap normal is a red herring: classloaders and their metaspace are held by a small object graph.
  4. How I'd verify each: Tomcat's "Find leaks" button in the Manager and the stop-time log; heap dump after 2 redeploys and in MAT use "Duplicate classes" and path-to-GC-roots on the old WebappClassLoader, excluding weak references; jcmd <pid> VM.classloader_stats (JDK 11) and jstat -gc Metaspace column; jcmd <pid> GC.class_stats (verify flags).
  5. Root cause: Pool threads (http-nio-8080-exec-N) belong to the container and survive redeploy. Each holds a ThreadLocalMap whose entry value is an RequestCtx object from the old webapp's class loader. Value to class to ClassLoader to all its classes: the whole old webapp stays reachable. The entry key is weak but the value is strong, and a thread-pool thread never exits. Tomcat renews threads and clears entries on stop for leaks it detects, but it cannot detect all cases (per the Tomcat memory-leak-protection notes), notably values reachable from classes in the shared loader.
Thread (container, lives forever)
  -> ThreadLocalMap.Entry[key weak, value STRONG]
        -> RequestCtx instance
              -> RequestCtx.class -> old WebappClassLoader
                    -> every class of old app (metaspace)
  1. Fix: Short term: restart instead of redeploy. Code: always try { ... } finally { CTX.remove(); } in a filter.
public void doFilter(ServletRequest rq, ServletResponse rs, FilterChain c) throws IOException, ServletException {
  RequestCtx.CTX.set(new RequestCtx(rq));
  try { c.doFilter(rq, rs); } finally { RequestCtx.CTX.remove(); }
}

Also ServletContextListener.contextDestroyed to deregister drivers, stop executors and Timers. 7. Prevention: CI deploy-redeploy-10x test checking Metaspace; static analysis (ErrorProne/Sonar) for ThreadLocal without remove; treat in-place redeploy as unsupported in prod. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not raising Metaspace (delays the failure). Not relying on WeakReference hacks. Containers with immutable images avoid the whole class of problem.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does ThreadLocal.remove() matter with a fresh thread per request? → No leak across requests then, but pooled threads make it mandatory.
  • Are InheritableThreadLocals worse? → Yes: child threads copy values and may outlive the request.
  • Why do virtual threads change this? → Threads are short-lived so leaks disappear with the thread, but per-thread caches stop being a cache.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "temporary" redeploy script lasted 4 years; the team found the leak only when a new library enlarged each webapp by 2x.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases metaspace.
  • Hire: explains ThreadLocal to classloader chain and removes in finally.
  • Strong hire: uses a heap dump to prove it, fixes the deploy model, and notes container detection limits.

questions.contextHtml: One of 12 pods of a pricing service (Java 17, 8 vCPU) sits at 780% CPU while the others are at 60%. Latency on that pod is 12 s, the load balancer keeps sending it traffic because the health check is a static /ping. GC log shows 5 ms young pauses every 20 s; heap is at 40%. No errors in the log. The pod was fine until a 11:40 config push that changed a promotion rule table.
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through finding the loop with the pod still running.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart it." That erases the evidence and does not answer why one pod.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the config differ per pod (one pod got a bad value)? Is CPU user or system time? Is it constant or oscillating?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Take the pod out of rotation (remove label/readiness failing), keep it alive for diagnosis; add real health checks later.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A tight application loop (bad config e.g. while (!done) or regex backtracking); (b) a corrupted HashMap spinning (see Q286); (c) GC thrash (ruled out by the log); (d) JIT compile storm.
  4. How I'd verify each: top -H -p <pid> to find the hottest native thread ID; convert to hex (printf '%x' 12345); jcmd <pid> Thread.print and match nid=0x...; repeat 3 times, 2 seconds apart: same frames means a loop, not a transient. Then async-profiler (asprof -e cpu -d 30 -f flame.html <pid>) for a flame graph, or JFR jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=/tmp/x.jfr.
  5. Root cause (example outcome): One thread in PromotionRule.evaluate spinning in a regex with nested quantifiers on a new config pattern (catastrophic backtracking: exponential in input length), while the other 7 cores were burned by retries piling more such requests. Only that pod got the push because of a partial rollout.
  6. Fix: Short term: revert the config; kill the pod after taking a dump. Long term: compile regex once, avoid ambiguous patterns, use linear-time engines like RE2/J for user-provided patterns, and add a timeout wrapper (a CharSequence that checks a deadline).
static CharSequence deadline(CharSequence s, long nanos) {
  long end = System.nanoTime() + nanos;
  return new CharSequence() {
    public char charAt(int i) {
      if (System.nanoTime() > end) throw new IllegalStateException("regex timeout");
      return s.charAt(i);
    }
    public int length() { return s.length(); }
    public CharSequence subSequence(int a, int b) { return s.subSequence(a, b); }
    public String toString() { return s.toString(); }
  };
}
  1. Prevention: Config validation and staged rollout with canary metrics, real readiness probes with a deep check and timeouts, per-request deadlines, alert on a pod's CPU being an outlier versus peers.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't kill -3 loops on a busy prod without knowing it writes to stdout; don't attach heavy profilers at default settings (async-profiler at 100 Hz or JFR default profile is cheap, sizeable -XX:+AllocationProfiling options are not). Don't restart before capturing.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does the hot thread's stack look in "RUNNABLE" but in native code? → Might be a JIT-compiled loop; the dump shows the Java frame at a safepoint, which can be biased (safepoint bias); profile with async-profiler to avoid it.
  • Counted loops without safepoint polls? → In older JVMs a long int counted loop could delay safepoints; mitigated by loop strip mining on modern JVMs (verify per release).
  • It's system CPU, not user? → Look at syscalls with strace -c/perf, check for GC threads or spin in epoll.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A regex fix of one character cut a pod from 780% to 15% CPU. The outage was prolonged because the health check never exercised the code.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts blindly.
  • Hire: top -H plus hex plus jstack.
  • Strong hire: also reasons about safepoint bias, profiles, finds the config trigger, fixes health checks and rollout.

questions.contextHtml:
A wallet service (Java 17, Tomcat) transfers money between accounts. Once or twice a week, a handful of requests hang forever; then the number of stuck threads grows by about 10 per minute until all 200 are stuck and the pod fails health checks. jcmd <pid> Thread.print ends with:

Found one Java-level deadlock:
"http-nio-exec-41": waiting to lock monitor 0x...(object 0x...a Account), which is held by "http-nio-exec-87"
"http-nio-exec-87": waiting to lock monitor 0x...(object 0x...a Account), which is held by "http-nio-exec-41"

The code was reviewed, and the lock is synchronized (from) { synchronized (to) { ... } }.
questions.promptHtml: Explain, fix permanently, and discuss how you would make it hard to reintroduce.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use tryLock with a timeout" without removing the cause, or "reduce concurrency".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are there other lock holders (DB row locks too)? Do transfers involve more than two accounts? Is there a unit of work larger than one JVM (multiple pods)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Take thread dumps first (evidence), then restart the pod; synchronized monitors cannot be interrupted, so the threads will not recover.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Inconsistent lock order, A to B in one request and B to A in another (the textbook deadlock: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait); (b) a lock plus DB row lock inversion that spans the JVM; (c) a lock held while calling an alien method.
  4. How I'd verify each: The dump itself reports Java-level deadlocks for monitors and ReentrantLocks (ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() can do it programmatically); correlate request IDs from MDC for the two threads (transfer 7->9 and 9->7); for the DB case, pg_locks/SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS.
  5. Root cause: Thread X does transfer(A,B) and thread Y transfer(B,A). X holds A and waits for B; Y holds B and waits for A. Four conditions met, so it never resolves; rarely hit because the window is tiny.
  6. Fix: Impose a global lock order, e.g. by account id; tie-break with an identity hash if ids can be equal.
void transfer(Account a, Account b, long amt) {
  Account first = a.id() < b.id() ? a : b;
  Account second = first == a ? b : a;
  synchronized (first) {
    synchronized (second) { a.debit(amt); b.credit(amt); }
  }
}

Better in a multi-pod world: do it in the database with a single transaction that locks rows in id order (SELECT ... WHERE id IN (...) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE) and drop in-JVM locks, which don't protect against other pods anyway. 7. Prevention: A deadlock watchdog (scheduled ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() alerting and dumping), a test with 2 threads opposite order and @Timeout, a lock-order convention in docs, and static checks. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: tryLock with timeout plus backoff avoids the hang but introduces livelock risk and needs a retry policy. A single global lock is correct but serializes everything. Don't catch and ignore the hang with request timeouts alone: monitors are not released.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why can't an interrupt save a synchronized waiter? → Monitor entry is not interruptible; lockInterruptibly() on ReentrantLock is.
  • Three accounts? → A total order on ids still prevents cycles.
  • Does a deadlock show in CPU metrics? → No: CPU idles; look for thread count growth and stuck request gauges.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A weekly hang was auto-restarted for 6 months, billed as "memory problem", until someone saved a dump before restart.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts only.
  • Hire: lock ordering with code.
  • Strong hire: also moves the invariant to the DB, adds the watchdog and test.

questions.contextHtml: A flash-sale API (Java 17, Spring Boot, 4 vCPU pods) autoscales on CPU at 70% from 6 to 60 pods during a 5-minute traffic ramp. New pods take 75 s to be Ready (Spring context 40 s, 12 s waiting on first DB connections, rest class loading) and then run slowly for 2 more minutes. The existing pods hit CPU 95% and p99 latency exceeds 4 s before capacity arrives; HPA launches pods in reaction, too late. Cost constraint: no always-on 60 pods.
questions.promptHtml: Make the system survive the ramp.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Lower the HPA CPU threshold" only, or "switch to Go".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How predictable is the sale (scheduled)? What is the allowed error budget? Max startup time target? Are DB connections the startup bottleneck (limits per pod)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pre-scale before the event on a schedule (KEDA cron / scheduled scaling), raise min replicas for the window, load-shed at the gateway.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Startup is dominated by Spring bean init and class loading; (b) JIT warmup after Ready; (c) DB or cache stampede as 54 pods connect; (d) HPA lag (metrics scrape interval + stabilization + scheduling + image pull).
  4. How I'd verify each: Startup log timestamps; -Xlog:startuptime style (JDK) / Spring Boot spring.main.lazy-initialization comparisons; Actuator startup endpoint (BufferingApplicationStartup) to find slow beans; -Xshare:auto -XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive for dynamic CDS (JDK 19+; verify flag availability on your JDK); JFR on startup.
  5. Root cause: Total time-to-capacity = HPA reaction (~1-2 min) + schedule + image pull + 75 s start + 120 s warmup, roughly 5 minutes, equal to the ramp length. Capacity arrives after the pain.
  6. Fix: Budget the 5 minutes: (1) pre-scale on schedule, plus scale on a leading indicator (request rate or queue depth, not CPU); (2) cut startup: AppCDS archive (reported around 40% faster startup in vendor material; measure), lazy init for rarely used beans, trimmed classpath, smaller connection init (initializationFailTimeout, staggered minimumIdle), (3) warmup gate and LB slow-start (see Q282); (4) consider CRaC or native image for the hottest service; (5) keep a standby ring via overprovisioning pods (low-priority placeholders).
-XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive -XX:SharedArchiveFile=/app/app.jsa   # JDK 19+, dynamic AppCDS
-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1   # NOT for steady-state: C1 only, faster warmup but ~lower peak
  1. Prevention: A scale-up game day with load generator (k6) reproducing the ramp; dashboards of time-to-ready and time-to-capacity.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't permanently run C1 only to save warmup; don't drop to 1 connection pool per pod blindly; native image trades peak throughput and observability.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why CPU is a poor HPA metric here? → It lags and saturates; scale on RPS per pod or in-flight requests.
  • Does lowering the HPA target to 40% just cost more? → Yes; use scheduled pre-scale for known peaks and a lower target only as buffer.
  • What if DB connections cap pod count? → Put a pooler (PgBouncer/RDS Proxy) and cap per-pod pool; bound pods.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team cut startup from 75 s to 30 s with AppCDS and lazy init, but the real win was scheduling scale-out 10 minutes before the known sale.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweak HPA threshold.
  • Hire: separates startup and warmup, pre-scales.
  • Strong hire: time-to-capacity budget, leading indicators, startup tech with trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml: A recommendations service (Java 17, G1) runs 40 pods of 8 GiB (6 GiB heap, 4 vCPU). Finance asks for a 40% cost cut. Current numbers: CPU 35% average, p99 120 ms (SLO 250 ms), heap after full mark is 1.4 GiB (live set), allocation rate 600 MB/s, young pauses 25 ms every ~4 s, G1 concurrent cycles rare. Proposal from the team: halve the heap to 3 GiB and halve pod count.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do and what do you check before approving?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Heap is mostly empty, just reduce it" without allocation rate or the live set math.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the peak-to-average ratio and failover headroom (N+1/AZ loss)? Is the live set stable over days? Any large caches? Throughput or latency bound at peak?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (not an incident). Start with a measured experiment on 2 canary pods, not the fleet.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Right-size memory first: live set 1.4 GiB so heap of ~3 GiB (live x 2-3) gives enough young room; (b) CPU is the real constraint when halving pods: doubling per-pod load raises CPU to ~70% and GC threads compete; (c) fewer, bigger pods raise failure blast radius; (d) lower heap shortens GC frequency headroom: with 600 MB/s allocation and young gen of, say, 1.2 GiB, a young GC every 2 s instead of 4 s.
  4. How I'd verify each: -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log and compare pause, frequency and Pause Young (Normal) times; GCeasy/GCViewer; check mixed collections and "to-space exhausted" and humongous allocations; JFR allocation profiling to see top allocators; load test at 1.2x of peak with k6 on canary; Micrometer jvm.gc.pause, jvm.gc.live.data.size, jvm.gc.max.data.size.
  5. Root cause of the opportunity: Over-provisioned memory (6 GiB for 1.4 GiB live) and low CPU use. The cost is dominated by pod count x memory, so the cheapest cut is memory per pod (pod 8 to 5 GiB with heap 3 GiB, leaving ~2 GiB for non-heap, see Q281), then consolidation from CPU data.
  6. Fix: Plan: Step 1: heap 3 GiB, container 5 GiB, -XX:MaxRAMPercentage replaced with explicit -Xmx3g -Xms3g; watch pause. Step 2: reduce allocation rate (the cheapest "GC tuning"): fix hot allocators found with JFR, e.g. avoid boxing, reuse buffers, don't re-serialize. Step 3: pod count from CPU headroom: target 55-60% peak CPU, N+1 capacity. Expected saving: memory 40% less per pod, pods 40 to ~28 (-30%): combined about 55-60% of the memory bill, ~35% of total after fixed costs (the math is rough; confirm with measure).
-Xms3g -Xmx3g -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/gc.log:time,uptime:filecount=5,filesize=20m
  1. Prevention: Keep the SLO dashboards on GC overhead (< 5% time), pause p99, live-set trend; re-check after each release (live set grows).
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not switching to ZGC/Shenandoah just for cost (they need headroom, use more CPU/memory overhead; generational ZGC in 21 helps but test); not cutting below live set x 2 (promotion failure -> Full GC); not tuning dozens of G1 flags without data.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Latency SLO becomes 50 ms? → Look at pause-time goal and maybe ZGC (verify generational ZGC availability: JDK 21+, default in 23+).
  • Heap shrink makes full GCs in a bursty hour. → Keep headroom for bursts, keep -Xms==-Xmx, and alert on to-space exhausted.
  • Sidecars count toward pod memory? → Yes; budget them.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team cut the allocation rate by 40% with two JFR-guided fixes, which allowed halving the heap with lower pauses than before.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: halves everything blindly.
  • Hire: uses live set, allocation rate and canary.
  • Strong hire: connects to container budget, N+1, allocation fixes and quantifies savings honestly.

questions.contextHtml:
An export service (Java 17, G1, 8 GiB heap, default region size = 4 MiB for this heap) shows GC pauses of 600-1100 ms every few minutes, while young pauses are ~30 ms. Log excerpt:

[gc] GC(412) Pause Young (G1 Humongous Allocation) 5100M->4900M(8192M) 780.234ms
[gc,heap] ... Humongous regions: 410->408

Traffic is steady at 300 RPS. A new endpoint builds a byte[] of the full CSV response (average 6 MB, some 80 MB) before writing.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase heap" or "switch GC", without recognizing humongous objects.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What region size? Rate of humongous allocations? Does heap occupancy rise just before the pause? Are objects short-lived or cached?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Flag off or rate-limit the endpoint; temporarily -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=16m so 6 MB arrays are no longer humongous (humongous = size >= 50% of region size).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Humongous allocation triggering early concurrent cycles/young GCs and fragmentation; (b) Full GC due to no contiguous free regions for big arrays; (c) a leak (heap grows after each GC? the log shows 5100->4900, stable); (d) IHOP adaptivity.
  4. How I'd verify each: -Xlog:gc+humongous=debug / -Xlog:gc*; jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info; JFR jdk.ObjectAllocationOutsideTLAB to locate the allocation site; confirm region size with jcmd <pid> VM.flags | grep G1HeapRegionSize.
  5. Root cause: Region size 4 MiB means any object >= 2 MiB is humongous: allocated directly in old-gen contiguous regions, reclaimed only at cleanup/ young GC end-of-marking (in JDK 17 eager reclaim for humongous objects exists for those with no incoming references, but not for the larger ones in certain cases; verify). Many 6-80 MB arrays fragment the old regions, trigger IHOP-driven concurrent cycles and evacuation failures, which are costly.
  6. Fix: Stream the CSV straight to the response (no giant buffer): code change fixes the cause. Config fallback: larger region size.
// before: byte[] all = buildCsv(rows); out.write(all);
try (var w = new BufferedWriter(new OutputStreamWriter(response.getOutputStream(), UTF_8), 64 * 1024)) {
  for (Row r : rows) { w.write(toCsv(r)); }   // bounded memory per request
}
  1. Prevention: Alert on humongous region count; guard rails on response size; review rule against "materialize whole result in memory".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Larger regions (max 32 MiB) waste memory on small heaps and reduce region count; not shifting to Parallel just because of the symptom.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• ZGC handles this better? → Large objects are allocated in dedicated large pages with no copying, but 80 MB per request is still a bad design.
  • Why did the pauses worsen over days? → Fragmentation of free regions.
  • Does Java 21 change this? → Check release notes; humongous handling has improved gradually (verify).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "CSV export" feature produced 1 s pauses that the on-call blamed on the database; GC logs showed Humongous Allocation in the cause field.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increase heap.
  • Hire: names humongous, adjusts region size.
  • Strong hire: streams response, verifies with logs/JFR, explains the regions arithmetic.

questions.promptHtml: An alert says "checkout p99 latency is 5x". You have 10 minutes before the incident call. Walk me through the first steps you take on a JVM service, and in what order.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors have a repeatable method; juniors guess. They are looking for triage before deep diving.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I check what changed (deploy, config, traffic), then use RED to see if errors, rate or duration moved and USE on the resources: CPU, memory, threads and pools, network, disk. If CPU is low and latency high, it's waiting: threads, locks, connection pools or a downstream. If CPU is high, profile; if memory, check GC. I mitigate first (rollback, shed load, scale) and take evidence (thread dump, JFR) before restarting."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
1 Scope:      one pod / all pods / one endpoint / one customer?   (outlier = bad host/config)
2 Change:     deploy, flag, config, dependency, traffic mix, cron/batch
3 RED:        Rate, Errors, Duration (per endpoint)
4 USE:        Utilization/Saturation/Errors per resource
              CPU(+throttling) | heap/GC | threads/pools queues | DB/HTTP pools | network | disk
5 JVM triage: GC log -> pause/frequency; jstack x3 -> blocked/waiting/RUNNABLE;
              pool metrics -> active=max & queue growing; JFR/async-profiler if CPU
6 Mitigate:   rollback / flag off / shed load / scale / restart the one bad pod (after dump)
7 Evidence:   save dumps, JFR, GC logs, timelines BEFORE restart
  • CPU low + latency high: waiting on something (pool, lock, downstream). CPU high + GC log busy: memory/GC. CPU high + GC quiet: hot code (profile).
  • Take 3 thread dumps 5-10 s apart: one dump is a photo, three show movement.
  • Use dependency metrics (client-side timers) to separate "we are slow" from "they are slow".

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
jcmd <pid> Thread.print > td1.txt; sleep 5; jcmd <pid> Thread.print > td2.txt
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=inc duration=60s filename=/tmp/inc.jfr settings=profile
jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000 10

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Restarting before capturing evidence.
  • Diving into GC tuning with no GC symptom.
  • Treating averages as truth (use percentiles).
  • Not checking for CPU throttling in containers (Q300).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if only one pod is bad? → Compare it with peers: config, node, noisy neighbor, a corrupted-state bug; isolate it and take dumps.
  2. Which dump tool is safe in prod? → Thread dumps and JFR are cheap; heap dumps pause the JVM (full GC and file write) so do it on an isolated pod.
  3. How do you write the mitigation vs root-cause split? → Mitigate in minutes with reversible actions; root cause after stability with evidence.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE jumps to the tool they know (GC logs or heap dump). Senior triages by symptom pattern, mitigates early, preserves evidence, and communicates.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team spent 40 minutes tuning G1 flags during a latency incident; the cause was an upstream DNS timeout visible in client timers within the first 5 minutes.

questions.contextHtml: A catalog service calls an inventory service (p99 80 ms, normally 800 RPS). Inventory gets a bad deploy and slows to 4 s. The catalog's HTTP client has read timeout 10 s, 3 retries (no backoff), Tomcat 200 threads, and the gateway in front has a 5 s timeout and also retries once. Within 90 seconds catalog threads are all blocked, its own p99 is 5 s (gateway timeouts), and inventory, which was recovering after a rollback, is flooded with ~4x its normal request rate and stays down for 25 more minutes. Outcome: a 35-minute outage for a feature that was meant to degrade gracefully.
questions.promptHtml: Write the post-incident review: causes, contributing factors, and the changes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Inventory's bad deploy was the root cause; add better testing." That misses the amplification mechanism.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Timeline of detection vs rollback? Were retries idempotent-safe? What do clients do on failure (fallback)? Were there circuit breakers? Which layer's retries applied?
  2. Immediate mitigation: (in the incident) Disable retries by flag, open a breaker manually, shed load at the gateway, serve cached inventory.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (contributing factors): (a) Retry amplification: gateway x catalog = (1+1)*(1+3) = 8 attempts per user request; (b) timeouts inverted: inner timeout (10 s) larger than the outer (5 s), so work continues after the caller gave up; (c) no bulkhead: all 200 threads shared between inventory and everything else; (d) no backoff/jitter, no retry budget; (e) no load shedding or breaker, and no fallback.
  4. How I'd verify each: Request count ratios in RED metrics (catalog->inventory rps vs user rps); traces showing nested retry spans; thread dump with threads in SocketInputStream.read/HttpClient; compare timeouts across layers in config.
  5. Root cause: An unbounded-failure coupling. Little's law says threads needed = rate x latency = 800 x 4 s = 3,200 concurrent calls vs 200 threads, so within seconds everything blocks. Retries multiplied the offered load so the dependency could not recover (metastable failure).
user -> gateway(5s, retry 1) -> catalog(10s, retry 3) -> inventory
attempts per user request: 2 x 4 = 8      concurrency = 800 x 8 x 4s ~ 25,600
  1. Fix: Deadline propagation (outer deadline decreases inner timeouts: each hop's timeout < caller's remaining time); retries only at one layer, with exponential backoff + jitter and a retry budget (e.g. retries <= 10% of requests); circuit breaker + bulkhead per dependency (semaphore or separate pool) so inventory can only use e.g. 40 threads; fallback to stale cache; Retry-After/429 respected.
// Resilience4j-style: bulkhead + breaker + time limit, retry only idempotent calls, with budget
Supplier<Stock> s = Decorators.ofSupplier(() -> client.stock(id))
    .withBulkhead(bulkhead)            // maxConcurrentCalls = 40
    .withCircuitBreaker(breaker)       // opens at 50% failures
    .withFallback(List.of(Exception.class), e -> cache.stale(id))
    .decorate();
  1. Prevention: Chaos/game-day: inject 4 s latency into each dependency; review checklist "timeout < caller's timeout, retries once, jitter, budget"; alerts on retry ratio.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not "retry harder" for availability; not removing retries entirely (transient errors are real); a circuit breaker can serve stale data, a business decision to agree on.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is a bigger thread pool not the fix? → It delays saturation and raises memory/context-switch cost, and still amplifies load on the dependency.
  • Hedged requests? → Useful for tail latency on idempotent reads but must be bounded or they add load.
  • What would virtual threads change? → No thread starvation, but concurrency becomes unbounded unless you cap it (Semaphore), and the dependency overload remains.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Two teams each added "just one retry" in different layers over two years; nobody owned the multiplication until the first dependency slowdown.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the deploy.
  • Hire: identifies retry amplification and timeouts.
  • Strong hire: does the math, proposes deadline propagation, retry budgets, bulkheads and drills.

questions.contextHtml:
A recommendation endpoint on a 4-vCPU pod (Java 17) runs this on every request (~200 RPS):

List<Product> enrich(List<String> ids) {
  return ids.parallelStream()
            .map(id -> inventoryClient.fetch(id))   // blocking HTTP call, ~120 ms
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
}

Under load: p50 is fine, but p99 is 9 s, and other endpoints that use parallelStream() or CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(...) without an executor also slow down at the same time. CPU is 20%. jstack shows ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1..3 blocked in socket reads.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and what are the fixes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Parallel streams are fast, so the HTTP client is slow."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism set? How many ids per request? Do other features use the common pool?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Replace by a dedicated bounded executor (or sequential) on the hot endpoint.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Blocking I/O in the common pool (parallelism = cores-1 = 3 workers + the calling thread, shared JVM-wide); (b) a request with 100 ids occupying the pool for 100 x 120 ms / 4 = 3 s, starving everything else; (c) the downstream is slow (check client metrics).
  4. How I'd verify each: jcmd <pid> Thread.print to count commonPool workers blocked; ForkJoinPool.commonPool().getParallelism()/getQueuedSubmissionCount() exposed as a gauge; JFR socket read events (jdk.SocketRead) from commonPool threads.
  5. Root cause: Parallel streams and un-parameterised supplyAsync share one pool sized for CPU work (cores - 1). Blocking calls park its few workers; unrelated tasks queue. Also, the caller thread participates and a slow task can hold up the whole stream, as there's no timeout.
  6. Fix:
private static final ExecutorService IO = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    16, 16, 0, TimeUnit.SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(200),
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());   // bounded; sized from Little's law

List<Product> enrich(List<String> ids) {
  var futures = ids.stream()
      .map(id -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> inventoryClient.fetch(id), IO)
                                  .orTimeout(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS))
      .toList();
  return futures.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList();
}

Or use a batch endpoint (fetchAll(ids)) to avoid N calls. On JDK 21 with virtual threads, Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() plus a Semaphore is the simpler option. 7. Prevention: Lint rule banning parallelStream() and executor-less async in services; metrics for common pool; code review "is this CPU-bound?". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't raise common pool parallelism globally (affects all users of the pool); don't make the pool unbounded.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Trick to run a parallel stream in a custom pool? → Submitting the terminal operation inside a custom ForkJoinPool works in practice but is an implementation detail; not guaranteed by the spec.
  • Why CallerRunsPolicy? → Backpressure: the caller works instead of queueing.
  • Ordering preserved? → collect to a list preserves encounter order even on parallel streams.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: One hidden parallelStream() in a rarely used admin path took down checkout latency whenever an admin ran a report.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the HTTP client.
  • Hire: identifies common pool starvation.
  • Strong hire: sizes the dedicated pool, adds timeout/bounds, mentions batching and virtual threads.

questions.contextHtml: A notification service (Java 17, G1, 4 GiB heap, 4 vCPU) uses Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8) to send emails through a provider whose throughput dropped from 300/s to 40/s. Producers (a Kafka listener and an API) enqueue 250 tasks/s. After 20 minutes, GC time goes to 60%, the heap is at 3.9 GiB, request latency rises to 30 s, and finally OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError. MAT shows 4.6 million FutureTask objects in a LinkedBlockingQueue, each referencing a 600-byte payload.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure, the fix, and the correct overload behavior.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the heap" or "use a cached thread pool".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are emails droppable, delayable, or must not be lost? Is the source replayable (Kafka offsets)? What does the provider tell us (429/slow)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause the Kafka consumer, scale out consumers or shed low-priority mail; restart with a bigger heap only to drain.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Arrival 250/s > service 40/s with an unbounded queue (a growth of 210/s x 600 B+overhead); (b) leak (no; MAT shows the queue); (c) GC misconfiguration (symptom, not cause).
  4. How I'd verify each: MAT dominator tree (queue as the retained set), queue size gauge via ThreadPoolExecutor.getQueue().size(), GC log showing live set growth after each full GC (a rising floor = real live data), producer vs completed rates.
  5. Root cause: newFixedThreadPool uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue, so execute never blocks or rejects and overload turns into memory growth; the GC death spiral is the secondary effect (live set near max heap means back-to-back full GCs and the "GC overhead limit exceeded"/OOM).
  6. Fix: Bounded queue + explicit overload policy, and backpressure to the source.
var pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 8, 0, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(500),
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());  // slows the Kafka poll loop instead of buffering

With Kafka: pause partitions (consumer.pause) when the queue is > 80% full and resume at 30%, commit offsets only after send. Add provider circuit breaker and a dead-letter topic. 7. Prevention: Ban Executors.new* factories in the codebase (ErrorProne/Sonar rule), expose queue depth and rejected count metrics, load test with a throttled provider. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: DiscardPolicy loses data silently; AbortPolicy needs the caller to handle RejectedExecutionException; CallerRunsPolicy can stall the poll loop beyond max.poll.interval.ms and trigger consumer rebalances (so pause/resume is cleaner).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How do you pick queue size? → Capacity of what you can afford to buffer = tolerated delay x service rate (e.g. 5 s x 40/s = 200).
  • What if mail must not be lost? → Persist (Kafka/outbox) and apply backpressure upstream; do not buffer in memory.
  • Why not newCachedThreadPool? → Unbounded threads: unable to create native thread or provider overload.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A queue depth graph that only went up for 20 minutes was visible to nobody because nobody had added it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: bigger heap.
  • Hire: bounded queue and policy.
  • Strong hire: backpressure to source, sizing math, replayability and the rebalance trap.

questions.contextHtml:
A Spring MVC service (Java 17) logs with a traceId stored in SLF4J MDC by a servlet filter, and authorizes using SecurityContextHolder (thread-local strategy). A refactor makes a controller do:

@GetMapping("/orders/{id}")
public CompletableFuture<Order> get(@PathVariable long id) {
  return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
    log.info("loading order {}", id);               // traceId missing in logs
    auditService.record(currentUser(), id);         // currentUser() reads SecurityContextHolder -> null, sometimes someone else's!
    return repo.load(id);
  }, ioPool);
}

After release: logs for those requests have no traceId, auditing sometimes shows anonymous, and once a security review finds user A's audit entry written under user B.
questions.promptHtml: Why, and how do you fix it correctly?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Pass the traceId as a parameter" for logs only, ignoring the security-context leak.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the pool shared and are its threads reused? Is any cleanup done in finally? Does the framework offer a task decorator?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the endpoint to synchronous; treat the wrongly attributed audit rows as a security incident.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Thread-locals do not travel to pool threads; (b) pool threads keep stale values from a previous task (if a task set context and did not clear), producing cross-user attribution; (c) propagation of the Authentication object leaking into a long-lived thread.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log the thread name and MDC contents on submit and in-task; a test that submits two tasks with different users on a pool of 1; look for context set in tasks without clearing.
  5. Root cause: ThreadLocal is per thread. The lambda runs on ioPool threads where no filter ran. If some other code on that thread populated the SecurityContext (e.g. a previous task's decoration) and did not clear it, a later task inherits it.
  6. Fix: Capture on submit, restore in the task, clear in finally, wrapping the executor once.
static Runnable wrap(Runnable r) {
  Map<String, String> mdc = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap();
  SecurityContext sc = SecurityContextHolder.getContext();
  return () -> {
    Map<String, String> prevMdc = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap();
    try {
      if (mdc != null) MDC.setContextMap(mdc); else MDC.clear();
      SecurityContextHolder.setContext(sc);
      r.run();
    } finally {
      SecurityContextHolder.clearContext();
      if (prevMdc != null) MDC.setContextMap(prevMdc); else MDC.clear();
    }
  };
}

In Spring: DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor / DelegatingSecurityContextRunnable and a TaskDecorator on ThreadPoolTaskExecutor; tracing libraries (Micrometer context-propagation) provide ContextSnapshot. Better: pass the user and trace id explicitly into the service method. 7. Prevention: Single place where executors are created with the decorator; tests with a 1-thread pool and 2 users; ban raw supplyAsync without executor. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't use InheritableThreadLocal for pools (copies only at thread creation, so stale); MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL for the security context has the same issue.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Virtual threads? → Each virtual thread has its own thread-locals but they are not inherited by new tasks from a pool-like executor; ScopedValue (preview in 21-24, finalized in 25: verify) gives immutable inherited context.
  • Reactive/coroutines? → Context travels via Reactor Context / CoroutineContext; thread-local bridging is needed (A1 covers).
  • Cost of copying MDC? → Small map copy per task; acceptable.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An audit trail written under the wrong user was found by a customer, not by a test; the "fix" had been to log less.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: parameters for log only.
  • Hire: wraps executor and clears in finally.
  • Strong hire: recognises the security implication, treats it as incident, adds tests.

questions.contextHtml: A pricing API (Java 17, G1, 4 GiB heap) restarts every ~30 hours because of OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space. GC logs show the live set after each mixed/full collection rising linearly by ~60 MiB/hour; young pauses stay 20-40 ms until the last 2 hours, when full GCs of 3-6 s appear. A deploy 3 days ago added a "price lookup cache" using a static Map<RequestKey, Price> and a dependency upgrade. Sizing the cache was never discussed. There is no heap dump yet because the OOM kill came from the liveness probe before the dump finished writing to a 2 GiB ephemeral volume.
questions.promptHtml: How do you get proof and fix it without risking prod?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Take a heap dump and look" without addressing the cost, the disk limit, and the method.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the key's cardinality? Is the cache keyed on something with unique-per-request fields (timestamp, requestId)? Are equals/hashCode correct? Which entries are accessed twice?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Scheduled rolling restart every 12 hours (known-bad but safe) and raise liveness timeout; disable the cache via flag.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Unbounded cache with high-cardinality keys; (b) key class lacks equals/hashCode so each lookup inserts a duplicate; (c) a listener/ThreadLocal/static collection in the upgraded library; (d) metrics label cardinality explosion (Micrometer tags).
  4. How I'd verify each: Class histogram diff: jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram | head -20 at t0 and t0+3h; if a class grows linearly it's the suspect. Heap dump on ONE pod taken out of rotation: jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump -all /dumps/h.hprof (the -all flag includes unreachable objects, default dumps live only) with a volume sized > heap; analyze in Eclipse MAT: dominator tree, "Leak suspects", path to GC roots (excluding weak/soft). -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps with a dedicated volume for the next OOM.
  5. Root cause (typical): RequestKey included requestTimestamp, so no key ever repeated: 100% miss, 100% insert, map grows forever, and a static reference keeps it alive from a GC root.
// buggy
static final Map<RequestKey, Price> CACHE = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();   // unbounded, static
record RequestKey(String sku, String region, Instant requestedAt) {}      // unique every call
  1. Fix: Bounded, expiring cache keyed only on what determines the result.
Cache<SkuRegion, Price> cache = Caffeine.newBuilder()
    .maximumSize(50_000).expireAfterWrite(Duration.ofMinutes(5))
    .recordStats().build();
  1. Prevention: Metrics on cache hit rate/size; code review "every cache has a bound, a TTL and a hit rate"; live-set-after-GC alert on slope; a soak test (6-8 hours) in staging.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: SoftReference caches make GC behavior unpredictable; they are not a size policy. Don't raise -Xmx: it just moves the time-to-OOM. Heap dumps pause the JVM and expose sensitive data: protect them.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A leak vs just a large steady live set? → A leak's floor after full GC keeps rising; a big live set plateaus.
  • Why does GC time explode at the end? → As live set approaches max, each collection reclaims less, so collections become back-to-back (GC death spiral).
  • Dump too big to analyze? → Use MAT on a machine with RAM > dump, or jcmd GC.class_histogram diffs, or JFR OldObjectSample with path-to-gc-roots.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cache added for performance caused a monthly outage because its key included a request timestamp; hit rate of 0% was visible on day one if anyone had graphed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases heap.
  • Hire: heap dump + MAT, bounded cache.
  • Strong hire: histogram diffs, safe dump procedure, key analysis, monitoring and soak tests.

questions.contextHtml: A service in Kubernetes (Java 17, G1) has CPU request 2, limit 2 on a 16-core node. JVM sees 2 CPUs. Latency p99 is 70 ms normally, but exhibits sharp 150-400 ms spikes every few seconds, correlated with traffic bursts, while average CPU shows 55%. GC pauses are 20 ms. Prometheus shows container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total / container_cpu_cfs_periods_total at 38%. The JVM runs 18 GC and compiler threads in addition to 40 request threads.
questions.promptHtml: Why does a 55%-CPU service stall, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "CPU is only 55% so it's not CPU."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Limit vs request? Kernel/cgroup version (v1 CFS vs v2 cpu.max)? Number of GC/compiler threads? Burst pattern?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise or remove the CPU limit (keep request), or add pods; this is the quickest proof.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) CFS quota throttling: a quota of 200 ms per 100 ms period is consumed in a burst across many threads, then all threads are frozen for the rest of the period; (b) GC worker threads (parallel, e.g. 16 on node view) burn quota in a stop-the-world; (c) noisy neighbors; (d) GC log pauses (ruled out).
  4. How I'd verify each: container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total; cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat (nr_throttled, throttled_usec); jcmd <pid> VM.info / -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal | grep -E 'ActiveProcessorCount|ParallelGCThreads|CICompilerCount'; JFR jdk.CPULoad.
  5. Root cause: The quota is time per period, not a core count: with 2 CPUs (200 ms / 100 ms), 40 busy threads running in parallel on 16 physical cores can consume 200 ms of CPU-time in about 12 ms of wall time, then the cgroup is throttled for ~88 ms. Averages hide it; p99 sees it. GC and JIT threads make it worse.
  6. Fix: Short term: remove the CPU limit (use requests for scheduling; this is a widely discussed trade-off) or set limit at 2x request; set -XX:ActiveProcessorCount and -XX:ParallelGCThreads/ConcGCThreads, -XX:CICompilerCount appropriately; reduce request thread counts to match CPU.
-XX:ActiveProcessorCount=4 -XX:ParallelGCThreads=4 -XX:ConcGCThreads=1   # illustrative, measure

Long term: size pods by measured CPU at p99 of per-100ms usage, not averages; use a burst-friendly quota (cpu.cfs_burst_us on supported kernels; verify). 7. Prevention: Alert on throttled ratio > 5%; load test with the real limits; document the policy. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No limit risks noisy neighbors (set quotas at the namespace level); don't set JVM processors above actual quota to "get more parallelism".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does the JVM adapt to the quota? → Yes, it derives CPU count from the cgroup quota (rounded up), then sizes GC/compiler threads from that.
  • Why does GC "pause" look longer than in logs? → Logged pause is safepoint time; throttling during or between affects wall time (check Total time for which application threads were stopped).
  • Fractional CPU (250m)? → The JVM sees 1 CPU; it may choose Serial GC (fewer than 2 CPUs or <1792 MB means non-server-class machine; verify).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team chased GC flags for two weeks, then a Grafana panel of throttling showed 40% of periods throttled; removing the limit fixed p99 in a day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "CPU is fine".
  • Hire: knows CFS throttling.
  • Strong hire: reads cgroup stats, tunes thread counts, and understands policy trade-offs.

questions.promptHtml: Latency is rising during peak. Someone proposes doubling the thread pool and the connection pool. How do you decide if it will help, and how do you size pools from first principles?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers reason with queueing math instead of guessing; many outages are caused by "bigger pools".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Little's law: concurrency L = arrival rate lambda x time in system W. A pool is just the allowed concurrency.
