If the bottleneck is CPU or the database, more threads only increase queueing and context switching; if threads mostly wait on I/O, I need threads = rate x wait time. I measure service time per resource, find the bottleneck by utilization and saturation, and size each pool to what the next stage can handle, with bounded queues."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• L = lambda x W. Example: 500 req/s with 200 ms average latency needs 100 in flight. If each request holds a DB connection for 40 ms of it, you need 500 x 0.04 = 20 connections, not 100.
  • CPU-bound pool: threads ~ cores (+1). I/O-bound: threads ~ cores x (1 + wait/compute). With 4 cores, 5 ms compute, 95 ms wait: 4 x (1+19) = 80.
  • Adding capacity before a bottleneck only moves the queue (to the DB, locks, GC). Past saturation, latency grows nonlinearly: M/M/1 mean wait ~ 1/(mu - lambda): at 90% utilization queue time is 10x service time, at 95% 20x.
  • Downstream limits cap upstream pools: total app connections = pods x pool size must stay under the database's capacity (and its efficient concurrency, often tens, not hundreds).
requests -> [HTTP threads 200] -> [DB pool 20] -> DB (efficient concurrency ~ 2*cores)
            ^ bigger here = longer queue at the pool, same throughput
  • Bounded queues give backpressure; unbounded queues convert overload into latency and then memory.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Back-of-envelope sizing helper
static int poolSize(double rps, double seconds) { return (int) Math.ceil(rps * seconds); }
// poolSize(500, 0.040) -> 20 DB connections; add ~20-30% headroom, then load test

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using average latency instead of p99 (tail needs larger buffer).
  • Forgetting multiplicative effects: pods x pool size.
  • Sizing pools by CPU count when the work waits on I/O (or the opposite).
  • Treating throughput gain from more threads as linear (Amdahl, contention, USL).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can more threads reduce throughput? → Context switches, cache misses, lock contention, and the downstream collapsing (Universal Scalability Law: contention and coherency terms).
  2. How do you choose a queue size? → Tolerated delay x service rate; reject or shed beyond.
  3. How does this change with virtual threads? → Threads are no longer the limit; the limiting resources (DB, remote services) must be capped explicitly via semaphores/pools.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE gives rules of thumb (cores x 2). Senior derives from rate x time, identifies the bottleneck resource, accounts for pods and downstream limits, and validates with load tests.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Pools raised from 20 to 200 in an incident turned a stuck service into a stuck database; the right move was shortening connection hold time.

questions.contextHtml:
A service refreshes a pricing cache every 30 s:

ScheduledExecutorService ses = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(1);
ses.scheduleAtFixedRate(() -> {
  cache.putAll(pricingClient.fetchAll());   // throws SocketTimeoutException once in a while
}, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

After a pricing blip at 03:12 the cache is never refreshed again. Prices served are 9 hours stale by morning. No error in logs, no alerts, the thread pool looks healthy, the app is up.
questions.promptHtml: What happened and how do you make it robust?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The network was down; add a retry." The real issue is the scheduler stopped.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there a staleness metric? Is serving stale prices acceptable, and for how long? Are other scheduled tasks on this executor?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart the pod or trigger a manual refresh; add a staleness check/page.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The periodic task threw an exception: per scheduleAtFixedRate docs, if any execution throws, subsequent executions are suppressed; (b) task blocked forever (no timeout) so later runs never start; (c) thread death with no replacement (not here: the pool replaces threads, the schedule is what is cancelled).
  4. How I'd verify each: Keep the returned ScheduledFuture and check isDone(); the exception is only visible via future.get(); thread dump to see if the worker is blocked in a socket read; add a gauge "seconds since last successful refresh".
  5. Root cause: An uncaught exception cancels the periodic task silently; the exception is captured in the ScheduledFuture that nobody reads.
  6. Fix: Catch everything inside the task; use timeouts on the client; record success timestamp; alert on age.
ses.scheduleWithFixedDelay(() -> {
  try {
    cache.putAll(pricingClient.fetchAll());   // client has 2 s timeout
    lastOk.set(System.nanoTime());
  } catch (Throwable t) {                       // keep the schedule alive
    log.warn("price refresh failed", t);
    failures.increment();
  }
}, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

scheduleWithFixedDelay avoids back-to-back catch-up runs after a slow one (AtFixedRate bunches runs, though it never runs concurrently). 7. Prevention: Wrapper utility for all scheduled jobs, metrics for last-success age, Spring @Scheduled users should check the error handler config (an ErrorHandler logs but Spring's default for repeating tasks suppresses the exception and continues; behavior differs from raw executors). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Catching Throwable includes OutOfMemoryError; for fatal errors rethrow or exit. Don't swallow without a metric.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Single-thread pool and one task hangs? → All scheduled tasks on it stall; use timeouts and separate pools.
  • Daylight saving / clock changes? → Executors use System.nanoTime, unaffected; cron schedulers are not.
  • Multiple pods refreshing? → Thundering herd on pricing; add jitter or leader election.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A refresh job died on the first timeout after a deploy, and stale prices ran for hours because uptime and health checks were green.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds a retry.
  • Hire: knows exceptions cancel periodic tasks, catches.
  • Strong hire: freshness metric, timeout, fixed delay vs rate, fatal error handling.

questions.contextHtml: A Spring service (Java 17, no hot redeploy, container 3 GiB, heap 1.5 GiB, -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize unset) grows RSS from 1.8 GiB to the limit over 3 days and is OOMKilled. jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary shows Class committed growing from 90 MB to 900 MB; jstat -class shows loaded classes going from 14,000 to 410,000 with unloaded stuck at 120. The only change last sprint: a feature that builds a Groovy-like rules script per tenant request with GroovyShell.evaluate(script), and a custom Proxy.newProxyInstance per request with a fresh ClassLoader.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose, fix, and explain why GC did not clean it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set MaxMetaspaceSize" (turns a kill into an OOM at a smaller size, without fixing it).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What generates classes (reflection, proxies, scripting, CGLIB, lambdas, JSP)? One class loader per request? Can the scripts be cached by content hash?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the feature flag; restart pods nightly; set -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m so it fails inside the JVM with a clear OOM (dumpable) instead of a silent kill.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Runtime class generation on every request (scripting engine compiles a new class per evaluate); (b) a new class loader per request that stays reachable (cache, thread-local, static registry); (c) CGLIB proxies recreated because of changing configuration; (d) JIT/code cache (different region).
  4. How I'd verify each: jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram with sorting to see classes like Script123456, $Proxy*; jcmd <pid> VM.classloader_stats; -Xlog:class+load / class+unload counts; MAT: group by class loader, "path to GC roots" on a loader; -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError also covers metaspace OOM.
  5. Root cause: Metaspace is freed only when a class loader becomes unreachable and a GC cycle unloads it. Each evaluate defined a new class in a new loader, and a static Map<Tenant, Binding> referenced the script instance, so none of the loaders were collectable. Class metadata lives in native memory (not heap), so heap dashboards stay normal while RSS rises.
  6. Fix: Cache compiled scripts keyed by hash (bounded, with eviction), share one loader per tenant; or avoid dynamic code (data-driven rules engine / expression library without class generation); clear any strong references so loaders unload.
private final Cache<String, Script> compiled = Caffeine.newBuilder().maximumSize(500).build();
Script script(String src) {
  return compiled.get(sha256(src), k -> shell.parse(src));   // one class per distinct source
}
  1. Prevention: Metrics jvm.classes.loaded, jvm.classes.unloaded, jvm.memory.used{id="Metaspace"}; alert on loaded count slope; code review for defineClass/scripting.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't raise the cap, don't call System.gc() hoping to unload; class unloading needs unreachable loaders. Note that G1 unloads classes during the concurrent cycle/full GC, so a quiet old gen can delay unloading even for garbage loaders: another reason to watch it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not just -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize? → Default is unlimited (limited by native memory), so the container kill comes first; setting it gives a fail-fast.
  • Lambdas and hidden classes? → Bounded by call sites, not per invocation.
  • Does AppCDS reduce metaspace? → It shares class metadata for archived classes across JVMs but not dynamic-generated ones.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A per-tenant scripting feature compiled the same rule 40k times a day; hashing the source cut classes from 400k to 900.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: caps metaspace.
  • Hire: connects class generation and unreachable loaders.
  • Strong hire: uses histograms and loader stats, caches compiled scripts, adds alerts.

questions.contextHtml: A fan-out service (Java 17, 2 GiB pod, -Xmx1g) logs java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread: possibly out of memory or process/resource limits reached. Heap and GC are healthy. jcmd <pid> Thread.print | grep -c '^"' returns 14,200. A code path does new Thread(() -> callPartner(x)).start() per downstream call (3 per request, partner latency recently 30 s instead of 300 ms), at 150 RPS. Pod pids.max is 4,096 via a cgroup limit.
questions.promptHtml: Why does this error say "memory," and what is the fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase heap" (it is a native/OS limit).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What limits apply: ulimit -u, cgroup pids.max, vm.max_map_count, container memory? Default -Xss?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart, disable the offending path, and make the partner call time out.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Unbounded thread creation proportional to slow dependency (150 RPS x 3 x 30 s = 13,500 concurrent threads, matching the 14,200 observed); (b) PID/thread limit reached before memory; (c) stack memory: 14,200 x 1 MiB virtual reservations (only touched pages count toward RSS, but still significant).
  4. How I'd verify each: ls /proc/<pid>/task | wc -l; cat /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.max pids.current; jcmd <pid> Thread.print grouped by stack (awk/jstack tools) to find the dominant creator; NMT "Thread" section.
  5. Root cause: Thread-per-call without bound. Little's law gives concurrency = rate x latency; when latency went 100x, thread count went 100x. The message says "out of memory" because pthread_create failed, which the JVM reports as OOM regardless of whether the limit was memory, PIDs, or map count.
  6. Fix: Bounded executor with timeouts and rejection; or virtual threads with a Semaphore limit on concurrent partner calls.
private final Semaphore partnerSlots = new Semaphore(100);
CompletableFuture<Resp> call(Req r) {
  return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
    try {
      if (!partnerSlots.tryAcquire(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) throw new RejectedExecutionException("partner saturated");
      try { return partner.call(r); } finally { partnerSlots.release(); }
    } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); throw new CompletionException(e); }
  }, ioPool).orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
}
  1. Prevention: Metric jvm.threads.live with alert; ban new Thread in review; load test with slow dependency.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't lower -Xss below what deep recursion needs (StackOverflowError); don't raise OS limits as the fix.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cached thread pool the same? → Yes: unbounded.
  • Does a smaller heap leave more room for threads? → Yes, in a fixed container; each thread also costs kernel memory.
  • Virtual threads and this error? → No platform thread per task, but unbounded virtual threads still hammer downstream and memory.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Thread count graph had been flat at 300 for a year, so no one alerted on it; a partner slowdown made it 14k in 4 minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes heap.
  • Hire: identifies unbounded threads.
  • Strong hire: explains the OS limit, does Little's law, bounds concurrency.

questions.contextHtml: Your team plans to move a Spring Boot 3.3 order service (Java 21, Tomcat, 400-thread pool, 12 pods, HikariCP 30 connections per pod, ~3,000 RPS total, p99 180 ms) to virtual threads to handle a projected 3x load without buying pods. Dependencies: Postgres (max 500 connections), a partner REST API with a rate limit of 2,000 RPS, Redis, and a legacy SDK using synchronized. Management wants "flip the flag next Friday".
questions.promptHtml: How do you plan and execute the migration?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set the flag and test." Misses the downstream limits and the staged rollout.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the service I/O-bound (what fraction of request time is waiting)? Which JDK exactly (21 vs 25 for pinning)? Which shared resources need caps? Are there thread-local-heavy libraries?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; keep a one-flag rollback (platform threads) and canary percent.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (what can go wrong): (a) Pinning on synchronized + I/O (21; Q287); (b) the limit moves from 400 threads to the DB pool (30) and the partner rate limit; concurrency is no longer bounded, so a burst of 10k virtual threads waits on Hikari; (c) ThreadLocal-based caches (e.g. per-thread SimpleDateFormat buffers) multiplied by thread count; (d) CPU-bound sections starve the carriers; (e) observability gaps (thread dumps, pool metrics).
  4. How I'd verify each: Load test at 3x with real libs; JFR jdk.VirtualThreadPinned; -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full in staging (21); jcmd Thread.dump_to_file -format=json; Hikari pending gauge; partner client metrics; check jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism.
  5. Root cause of risk: Platform-thread pools were implicit bulkheads; moving to one thread per request removes that protection while the scarce resources (DB connections, partner QPS, CPU) remain.
  6. Fix (plan):
    • Step 1: add explicit limits (Semaphore/bulkhead per dependency; Hikari connectionTimeout 1-2 s; rate limiter for the partner at 1,800/s).
    • Step 2: staging soak with JFR pinning check; upgrade to a JDK where the pinning is solved or isolate the legacy SDK in a small platform-thread pool.
    • Step 3: canary 1 pod, then 10%, 50%, 100% over a week, comparing p99, error rate, DB wait, GC and thread counts; keep rollback by flag.
    • Step 4: only then reduce pods or grow load.
spring.threads.virtual.enabled: true
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size: 30
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout: 1500
  1. Prevention: Dashboards for virtual-thread-specific signals (pinned events, carrier utilization), "no synchronized around I/O" dependency review, synthetic load tests.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't pool virtual threads; don't expect more throughput if the DB is the bottleneck (then it's just a longer queue); don't skip the canary for the Friday deadline.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not just enlarge the platform pool to 2,000? → 2,000 x ~1 MiB stacks reserved plus context switching; viable but virtual threads are cheaper for blocking I/O.
  • Scoped values or ThreadLocal for request context? → ThreadLocal still works; ScopedValue finalized in a later JDK (verify version) to avoid copies.
  • CPU-bound endpoints? → No benefit, may hurt fairness (no time slicing).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration quadrupled concurrent DB waiters at peak because no one capped the pool; the DB, not Java, fell over.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: flips the flag.
  • Hire: identifies pinning and the DB pool limit.
  • Strong hire: staged canary, explicit bulkheads, rollback, metrics and honest expected gain.

questions.contextHtml:
During a TV-ad spike traffic goes from 600 to 6,000 RPS (10x). A search service (Java 17, G1, 6 GiB heap, 4 vCPU pods, autoscaling reached 20 pods in 7 minutes) experienced a 22-minute degradation. Timeline from logs:

12:01 Pause Young (Normal) 28ms every 3.2 s
12:04 Pause Young (Concurrent Start) ... to-space exhausted  210ms
12:05 Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 5800M->4100M(6144M) 6120ms
12:06 Pause Full ... 5900M->4800M 7900ms  (Full GCs back-to-back)
12:06 health check timeouts, pods removed from the LB, traffic shifts to survivors

Live set normally 1.8 GiB; during the spike each request builds up to 3 MB of intermediate results, and a result cache grows (maximumSize 200k entries x ~10 KB).
questions.promptHtml: Write the review: what failed, what you change in the JVM, the code and the platform.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Not enough memory, increase heap and add pods earlier."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What was the allocation rate before and during? Was cache entry weight bounded by count only? Why did the health checks remove nodes (cascade)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: (in the incident) Shed load at the edge, disable cache population, scale out, remove the full-GC'ing pods only after they stop receiving traffic to avoid shifting load.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Allocation rate outran concurrent marking: G1 starts marking at IHOP (default 45% of heap, adaptive), but with high rate the old gen filled before mixed collections reclaimed space, causing "to-space exhausted" evacuation failure then a Full GC (single-threaded in 17? Full GC is parallel since JDK 10: verify, still STW); (b) per-request garbage 3 MB x concurrent requests inflated young survivors, which premature-promoted to old (survivor overflow); (c) cache 200k x 10 KB = 2 GB (count-bounded, not weight-bounded) plus 1.8 GiB base live set leaves little room; (d) health checks tied to GC pause amplified into a cascade.
  4. How I'd verify each: GC log analysis (GCeasy): allocation rate, promotion rate, survivor tenuring distribution (-Xlog:gc+age=trace), time between marking start and finish, Evacuation Failure entries; JFR jdk.GCPhasePause, jdk.ObjectAllocationSample; heap dump at the 5800M point (on an isolated pod) to see cache and request buffers.
  5. Root cause: The service was sized for 600 RPS; at 10x, offered allocation ~ 6,000 x 3 MB = 18 GB/s... (the real number must be measured; even a fraction exceeds young capacity) so objects survived collections because request lifetimes (200-400 ms) exceeded the interval between young GCs (< 1 s). Premature promotion filled old gen; a count-bounded cache added ~2 GB; marking could not keep up; to-space exhaustion triggered Full GCs; health checks then removed healthy-but-paused pods, concentrating load (cascading failure).
  6. Fix: Immediate: cap by weight, not count (maximumWeight), reduce per-request intermediate result (stream/paginate), lower IHOP via -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=30 and -XX:G1ReservePercent=20 as insurance (verify effects with logs), more heap headroom, larger young via -XX:G1NewSizePercent; Platform: autoscale on request rate/in-flight, pre-scale for known ads, load shedding (concurrency limiter) so the service rejects instead of collapsing; health check separates liveness from readiness and does not fail on one slow response; Long term: evaluate generational ZGC (JDK 21+) for allocation-heavy bursts and measure.
Cache<Key, Result> c = Caffeine.newBuilder()
    .maximumWeight(256L * 1024 * 1024).weigher((k, v) -> v.sizeBytes()).build();
  1. Prevention: Spike load test at 10x with the production heap; alert on to-space exhausted, old-gen after-GC trend, GC time ratio; concurrency limiter per instance (Little's law: max in-flight = heap budget / per-request memory).
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not just increasing the pod heap (longer Full GCs, 6 s => 12 s); not removing health checks; ZGC/Shenandoah need CPU headroom; lowering IHOP raises GC CPU in steady state.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Is it a leak? → The floor was 1.8 GiB before and returned after the spike; a leak would not recover.
  • Admission control formula? → in-flight cap = usable heap for requests / peak per-request memory (e.g. 1.5 GiB / 3 MB = 500).
  • Why do Full GCs back-to-back? → Reclaimed too little, allocation immediately fills again.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The spike was predicted by marketing a week earlier; the only missing step was a 10x rehearsal.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more memory.
  • Hire: explains to-space exhaustion/premature promotion, fixes cache and sizing.
  • Strong hire: cascading health-check issue, admission control math, tests, and measured JVM changes.

questions.promptHtml: Which JVM diagnostic tools are safe to use on a live production pod serving traffic, which are risky, and how do you gather evidence without making the incident worse?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates who know the tools but not their cost are dangerous on call.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Cheap and generally safe: GC logs, JFR (default/profile settings), jcmd Thread.print, jstat, jcmd GC.class_histogram (short pause), async-profiler at moderate frequency. Risky: heap dumps (STW and large I/O, memory spike), jmap -histo:live (forces a full GC), attaching debuggers, -Xcomp, heavy allocation profiling. I take the risky ones from one pod removed from rotation, with enough disk, and keep dumps secured."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Tool Cost on a live JVM Notes
GC logging (-Xlog:gc*) negligible enable always, with rotation
JFR continuous (default ~1% overhead per Oracle docs; verify) low profile setting a bit higher
jcmd Thread.print short safepoint, scales with threads take 3 samples
jstat -gcutil negligible reads shared perf data
jcmd GC.class_histogram stops the world briefly; by default counts live objects only (triggers a full GC unless -all) verify per JDK
jmap -histo:live full GC avoid when heap is large
jcmd GC.heap_dump STW proportional to heap; writes file about heap size isolate pod, check disk
async-profiler (cpu/alloc/lock) low at 10 ms interval; no safepoint bias needs perf_events permissions in containers
NMT summary ~5-10% overhead if on detail; summary less (verify) must be set at startup
Remote debugger/breakpoints freezes threads never
  • Safepoint bias: jstack-style sampling only observes threads at safepoints; JFR and async-profiler use asynchronous sampling and avoid most of this.
  • Evidence checklist before restart: 3 thread dumps, GC log, JFR 60 s, class histogram, metrics snapshot, dmesg for OOM kills, recent deploy info.
  • Security: heap dumps contain secrets and PII; store encrypted, short TTL.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=inc settings=profile duration=60s filename=/tmp/inc.jfr
asprof -e cpu -d 30 -i 10ms -f /tmp/cpu.html <pid>
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump -all /dumps/inc.hprof    # only on an isolated pod with free disk >= heap

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Running jmap -dump on the only unhealthy pod still receiving traffic.
  • Filling the node's ephemeral storage with a dump, killing neighbors.
  • Enabling -XX:+PrintCompilation or heavy flags at default in prod.
  • Assuming kill -3 goes to a log you can reach in a container.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why continuous JFR? → Evidence exists before the incident; a ring buffer (maxage) with dump-on-exit.
  2. How to profile when the container lacks ptrace/perf? → Use JFR (no extra privileges), or grant narrow capabilities in a debug pod.
  3. What if the JVM is hung and jcmd can't attach? → Attach uses a signal and a socket; a hung process may not answer; use kill -3 (thread dump to stdout), gdb/jhsdb on a core, or a container-level core dump.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE knows jstack and jmap. Senior knows the cost of each, preserves evidence, uses always-on telemetry, and plans for the failure path (disk, security).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A heap dump on a loaded pod paused it for 40 s, failed liveness, and the restart destroyed the dump, a double loss.

questions.contextHtml: A product manager pings you: "The API feels slow sometimes, customers are complaining, fix it before the board demo on Thursday." Facts available: p50 is 45 ms, p99 is 600 ms, p99.9 is 4 s; the service is a Java 17 Spring Boot app, 10 pods, G1 with 4 GiB heap, Postgres, one partner API. No SLO document. Complaints cluster around "weekday mornings" but no endpoint, customer or timestamp is given. There is a JFR-less setup, metrics only in Prometheus (RED + JVM + Hikari), no tracing.
questions.promptHtml: How do you proceed from this vague request to a defensible outcome in 3 days?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Start tuning GC flags or adding caches without defining "slow" or collecting data.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which endpoints/customers/times; what threshold is "slow" (define an SLO, e.g. p99 < 300 ms for 99% of minutes)? What changed recently? Is the demo path known (focus on it)? What is the business cost of a slow request?
  2. Immediate mitigation: For the demo: identify the demo flow, pre-warm caches/pods, freeze deploys, and add a canary check. For general: nothing risky yet.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Morning traffic ramp + autoscaling lag => cold pods/JIT (Q282, Q291); (b) a slow partner call or DB query hitting the tail (p99.9 4 s smells like timeouts/retries); (c) GC or CPU throttling pauses (Q300); (d) connection pool waits (Q285); (e) lock contention. Don't commit until data.
  4. How I'd verify each: Day 1: build the data: slice latency by endpoint, pod, minute; correlate with deploys, HPA events, GC pause (jvm.gc.pause), Hikari pending, throttling ratio, partner client timers; turn on continuous JFR and add trace IDs (OpenTelemetry) for the slow requests; sample slow-request logs (log when > 1 s with phase timings). Day 2: reproduce with k6 replaying the morning pattern; test hypotheses one at a time. Day 3: fix the top one or two and measure.
  5. Root cause (example outcome): After correlation: p99.9 spikes align with pods less than 3 minutes old and with partner timeouts of 3 s plus one retry (4 s). Two causes, two fixes.
  6. Fix: Warmup gate + LB slow-start (Q282); partner timeout 800 ms, retry budget, circuit breaker (Q295); report before/after with the same dashboards. Communicate: "we cut p99.9 from 4 s to < 1 s for X; the remaining tail is Y, planned".
  7. Prevention: Define SLOs and error budgets, burn-rate alerts, tracing, a weekly latency review, and a "slow request" runbook.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not promise "fixed" without a metric definition; not changing five things at once (can't attribute); not tuning flags without evidence; not optimizing the average (p50) when the complaint is about the tail.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The PM says Thursday is fixed, but the cause is not found. → Reduce risk for the demo path (pre-warm, dedicated capacity, stable build), state what is known vs unknown, and keep investigating.
  • Metrics show nothing abnormal. → The averages lie; look at per-pod p99, client-side timing, and the load balancer's view; add tracing; possibly the issue is outside the service (DNS, TLS, CDN).
  • How do you set the SLO? → From user impact and current baseline; start with p99 per key endpoint and a 99% minute-compliance target.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: "Sometimes slow" turned out to be one pod on a node with a noisy neighbor; per-pod p99 panels found it in 10 minutes after two days of tuning the whole fleet.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes blindly or says "need more info" and stalls.
  • Hire: defines the symptom, slices data, forms hypotheses, and tests.
  • Strong hire: sequences a 3-day plan, protects the demo, communicates uncertainty, introduces SLOs and observability.
